title: UV Lights for Commercial HVAC Systems
h1: Are UV Lights Worth It for Commercial HVAC Systems?
description: UV-C lights keep coils and drain pans cleaner in commercial HVAC systems. Learn where they're installed, what they help with and how to maintain them safely.
quick_answer: UV-C lights in commercial HVAC systems are mainly used to keep cooling coils and drain pans free of mold and bacterial growth. That helps the coil stay cleaner, reduces musty odors and supports steady airflow. They work best as part of a maintenance plan that also includes good filtration, regular coil cleaning and scheduled lamp replacement.
body:
Offices, schools, medical offices, restaurants and retail spaces all depend on HVAC systems that run long hours. The coils inside those systems stay cold and wet during cooling, and over time they can collect growth that hurts airflow and causes odors. UV-C lights are one of the tools facility managers use to keep that in check.

How do UV lights work in commercial systems?

UV-C light damages the genetic material of mold, bacteria and other microorganisms so they can't grow. In a commercial system, lamps are typically mounted inside the air handler or rooftop unit, aimed at the cooling coil and drain pan. Because the coil and pan are always in the light, growth has a hard time starting.

Some systems also use lamps in the airstream to treat moving air. Air passes the lamps quickly, though, so this is less effective than coil treatment unless the system is designed for enough exposure time.

Where are UV lights usually installed?

  • Rooftop package units, which are common on offices, retail and restaurants in Southern California
  • Air handlers in mechanical rooms for larger buildings and schools
  • Split systems with indoor units in ceilings, closets or attics in smaller offices
  • Fan coils in multi-room facilities

The right lamp size and placement depend on the coil size and the layout inside the unit. A survey of the equipment comes before any recommendation.

What are the benefits for a business?

  1. Cleaner coils. Less growth on the coil helps it move heat efficiently and keeps airflow up.
  2. Fewer drain problems. Treating the drain pan reduces the slime that clogs lines and causes overflows into ceilings.
  3. Fewer odor complaints. Musty smells from the coil are a common complaint in offices and classrooms.
  4. Less frequent heavy coil cleaning. Coils still need regular service, but they tend to stay in better shape between visits.
  5. Support for indoor air quality goals. Keeping the coil clean removes one source of mold spores in the system.

What do UV lights not do?

UV lights don't filter dust, pollen or smoke. They don't replace regular coil cleaning when there's already buildup, and they don't fix drainage, humidity or ventilation problems. They also only treat what the light reaches. For particles, you still need good filtration, and for fresh air, the outdoor air settings need to be right.

During wildfire smoke events, for example, filtration and outside air control matter far more than UV.

How should UV systems be maintained?

A UV light that isn't maintained stops doing much. Build these into your service plan:

  • Replace lamps on the manufacturer's schedule, usually around once a year, even if they still glow
  • Clean lamps and sleeves when they get dusty
  • Check that the coil and pan are still fully covered by the light
  • Confirm that safety interlocks turn lamps off when access panels open
  • Recycle old lamps properly, since many contain mercury

What about safety for staff and technicians?

UV-C light can injure eyes and skin. Lamps inside HVAC equipment should be shielded from view and wired to shut off when a panel is opened. Label the units so anyone servicing them knows UV lamps are inside. Choose lamps that don't produce ozone, since ozone can irritate the lungs and isn't something you want in an occupied building.

Is UV right for your building?

UV coil treatment is often worth it in buildings with past odor complaints, recurring drain clogs, high humidity, long run hours or occupants who are sensitive to air quality, such as schools and medical offices. Buildings near the coast, where marine humidity keeps coils damp, are also good candidates.

Our commercial HVAC team surveys rooftop units and air handlers, installs UV systems sized for each unit, and can fold lamp replacement into your regular maintenance schedule. For more on how UV fits into an air quality plan, see our indoor air quality services.

For multi-unit sites, it often makes sense to start with the units that serve the most sensitive or most complained-about areas, then expand once you see the results.
faqs: Do UV lights reduce HVAC energy use?

They can help indirectly. A clean coil transfers heat better and keeps airflow steady, so the system doesn't work as hard. The bigger savings come from avoiding a dirty, clogged coil in the first place.
How many UV lamps does a rooftop unit need?
It depends on the coil size and the inside layout of the unit. Larger coils may need several lamps to cover the full face. A technician should size the system after looking at the equipment.
Can UV lights replace coil cleaning?
No. They reduce growth but don't remove dust, grease or existing buildup. Coils still need inspection and cleaning as part of regular maintenance.
Are UV lights safe in occupied buildings?
Yes, when installed inside the equipment, shielded from view and wired to shut off when a panel opens. Choose ozone-free lamps and label units so technicians know they're there.
